title: Blessings all day
hook: a rabbi of the Talmud taught a hundred blessings a day, scattered through the ordinary hours

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was counting the Omer: seven weeks of days, counted aloud one by one. Your line was count the days.

A hundred. That's the number Rabbi Meir named. A person, he taught, as the Talmud records, is obliged to say a hundred blessings every day. Not a hundred long prayers in a service. A hundred short sentences, scattered through the ordinary hours: on waking, before bread, after washing the hands, on hearing thunder. A hundred sounds like a great deal, until you see how small each one is, and how many things in an ordinary day could be stopped for and noticed.
screen: `A HUNDRED, SAID RABBI MEIR.` → `SHORT, AND SCATTERED.` → `WAKING, BREAD, THUNDER.`

segments.voice: You met the Jewish blessing back on day two hundred fifty; today, a whole day of them. A beracha has a shape people come to recognize. It opens by speaking to God directly, blessed are you, Lord our God, king of the universe, then names what's in front of the person: the one who brings bread from the earth, the one who creates the fruit of the vine. The Mishnah gives a whole chapter to blessings for things a person might meet: lightning and thunder, mountains and the sea, good news, and bad news too. The Talmud records a blessing for after using the bathroom, thanking God for a body made with openings that work as they should. Nothing is too ordinary to be noticed. A blessing comes before or alongside the thing, so it works like a small door. You don't just eat the apple. You stop, see that there is an apple, name where it came from, and then eat. The Talmud makes a striking claim: whoever enjoys something of this world without a blessing is like someone who has taken what belongs to heaven. The verse it leans on is from the Psalms, in the King James: "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof." Read this way, a hundred blessings is less a quota than a way of walking through a day with the doors open.
screen: `THE SHAPE OF A BLESSING.` · `THUNDER, MOUNTAINS, BAD NEWS.` · `A SMALL DOOR BEFORE THE THING.` · `ENJOYING WITHOUT A BLESSING.` · then, large: `THE EARTH IS THE LORD'S.`

segments.voice: Look around slowly for five things: the chair under you, the air coming in, a sound from outside, your own hands, the light in the room, and stay with each long enough to really see it. If you pray, you can use the old opening, blessed are you, and name the thing; if you don't, simply say a quiet thank you for it inside. Five small stops.
Blessings all day. Short Jewish blessings, scattered through the ordinary hours, a hundred of them in Rabbi Meir's teaching. Today's word.
Your line: a hundred blessings. By evening, a person has stopped a hundred times to notice something given. That's day one thousand three hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Observant Jews say short blessings throughout the day, on waking, before and after eating, after using the bathroom, and on seeing or hearing things like thunder, the sea or good news, aiming for a hundred a day.

chat.says: Why would anyone say a blessing before eating something as ordinary as an apple?
options: It's a small door: you stop, see the apple, and name where it came from.
It's mostly a way of asking that the food won't make you sick.
Only big meals need one; something as small as an apple doesn't count.

The blessing formula (baruch atah Adonai Eloheinu melech ha-olam) and the endings for bread (hamotzi) and wine (borei pri hagafen) are described in English without quotation marks, as a description of a real blessing, not a new one. Confirm the rendering.
Mishnah Berakhot 9:1–2: blessings on lightning, thunder, mountains, seas, good news and bad news; summarized. Confirm.
Asher yatzar (Berakhot 60b) summarized as 'a body made with openings that work as they should'; confirm tone is appropriate.
Berakhot 35a: one who benefits from this world without a blessing is as if he misused consecrated property (me'ilah), derived from Psalm 24:1; paraphrased as 'taken what belongs to heaven'. Confirm.
